{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01TDuMVgNLYG1JuNBcWceCS4","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections below in this order. Headings may be renamed slightly to suit the domain, but keep the order and intent. For small systems, a section may be a single sentence. If a section does not apply, keep its heading and give a one-line reason. Prefer tables where the notes suggest them.\n4\t\n5\t---\n6\t\n7\t## 1. Summary\n8\t\n9\tFive to ten sentences or a tight bullet list covering:\n10\t\n11\t- What is being built and for whom.\n12\t- The overall shape of the architecture in one or two sentences.\n13\t- The three to five most important decisions.\n14\t- What the first milestone delivers.\n15\t- The top risks.\n16\t\n17\tSomeone who reads only this section should know what is about to happen and why.\n18\t\n19\t## 2. Context and Goals\n20\t\n21\t- **Problem:** what is painful or missing today, and for whom.\n22\t- **Goals:** the outcomes the system must achieve, in measurable terms where possible.\n23\t- **Non-goals:** things deliberately left out of scope, so nobody assumes they are coming.\n24\t- **Success measures:** how you will know it worked after launch, such as adoption, latency, cost, accuracy, or time saved.\n25\t\n26\t## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n27\t\n28\t- **Ranked quality attributes:** a table with the columns *attribute*, *measurable target*, and *why it matters*, in priority order. Mark targets you inferred as assumptions.\n29\t- **Key functional requirements:** the capabilities that shape the structure. This is not a full backlog.\n30\t- **Constraints:** existing stack, hosting, team size and skills, deadline, budget, compliance, data residency, and mandated vendors.\n31\t- **Hard parts:** the few areas that are new, uncertain, dependent on outside parties, or costly to get wrong, each with one sentence on why.\n32\t\n33\t## 4. Current State\n34\t\n35\tWhat exists today that this work touches: relevant code, services, data stores, infrastructure, and processes. Cite specific files, modules, or systems where you inspected them. Note conventions the plan will follow. For entirely new builds, state what organisational or platform context applies.\n36\t\n37\t## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n38\t\n39\t- **Assumptions:** a table with the columns *assumption*, *impact if wrong*, and *how and when it will be validated*.\n40\t- **Open questions:** each with the owner or person who can answer it, the default you will use if no answer arrives, and the date or milestone by which it must be resolved.\n41\t\n42\t## 6. Architecture Overview\n43\t\n44\t- A text-based diagram (Mermaid or ASCII) showing components, data stores, external systems, and trust boundaries.\n45\t- A short narrative of how the parts fit together.\n46\t- A **component table** with the columns *component*, *responsibility*, *owns which data*, *exposes which interfaces*, *technology*, and *key dependencies*.\n47\t\n48\t## 7. Component Details\n49\t\n50\tFor each significant component:\n51\t\n52\t- Its responsibility and its boundaries, meaning what it explicitly does not do.\n53\t- Its interfaces: whether they are synchronous or asynchronous, the contract format, how they are versioned, and the expected load.\n54\t- Its internal structure, where that matters.\n55\t- How it fails and how it recovers.\n56\t- How it scales, if scale is a driver.\n57\t\n58\tRoutine components can be covered in a line or two.\n59\t\n60\t## 8. Data Design\n61\t\n62\t- The main entities and how they relate to each other.\n63\t- The system of record for each entity, and which component writes to it.\n64\t- Consistency requirements and where transactions are needed.\n65\t- Access patterns and the indexing or partitioning they imply.\n66\t- Retention, deletion, backup, and restore targets.\n67\t- Data classification, covering sensitive fields and how they are protected.\n68\t- How schemas will evolve and how migrations will be done.\n69\t\n70\t## 9. Key Flows\n71\t\n72\tWalk through the two to four most important scenarios step by step, from trigger to outcome. Use sequence diagrams or numbered steps. Include at least one failure path, such as a timeout, retry, duplicate, partial failure, or dependency outage, and show how the system behaves.\n73\t\n74\t## 10. Key Decisions\n75\t\n76\tOne entry per significant decision, optionally as a table:\n77\t\n78\t- **Decision:** what was decided.\n79\t- **Options considered:** at least two realistic ones.\n80\t- **Rationale:** why this option, measured against the ranked drivers.\n81\t- **Reversibility:** whether it is hard or easy to undo.\n82\t- **Revisit if:** the evidence or condition that would reopen the decision.\n83\t\n84\t## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n85\t\n86\tA short subsection for each. Name the concrete mechanism and the milestone in which it is built.\n87\t\n88\t- **Security:** identity, authorisation model, secrets, encryption, input validation, the main threats and their mitigations.\n89\t- **Reliability:** availability and recovery targets, redundancy, timeouts, retries, idempotency, backpressure.\n90\t- **Observability:** logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts tied to user-facing symptoms.\n91\t- **Performance and capacity:** expected load, the bottlenecks you expect, and how they will be load-tested.\n92\t- **Cost:** estimated run cost, the main cost drivers, and the controls on spend.\n93\t- **Operations:** who owns the system, runbooks, on-call expectations, and how support works.\n94\t- **AI-specific concerns, where relevant:** evaluation approach, guardrails, cost and latency budgets, human approval points, and the fallback when the model fails.\n95\t\n96\t## 12. Build Sequence\n97\t\n98\tA milestone table or list. For each milestone:\n99\t\n100\t- **Goal:** the risk it clears or the value it delivers.\n101\t- **Scope:** what is included and what is explicitly excluded.\n102\t- **Deliverables:** the concrete artefacts, features, or environments it produces.\n103\t- **Exit criteria:** checkable conditions that mark it complete.\n104\t- **Dependencies:** what must be finished first, and what can run in parallel.\n105\t- **Rough size:** a range, with the team assumption behind it.\n106\t\n107\tThe first milestone must contain a thin end-to-end slice and the spikes for the highest-risk unknowns. Mark the critical path.\n108\t\n109\t## 13. First Milestone Task Breakdown\n110\t\n111\tA list of concrete tasks. Each one has a verb and a deliverable, its location (module, directory, service, or repository), and a \"done when\" condition. Note the order and which tasks can run in parallel. Spikes include the question being answered, a time box, and the result that would change the plan.\n112\t\n113\t## 14. Testing and Validation Strategy\n114\t\n115\t- Which kinds of tests cover which risks: unit, contract, integration, end-to-end, load, security, and evaluation sets for AI components.\n116\t- The test environments and test data needed.\n117\t- What runs in CI and what blocks a release.\n118\t- How the measurable targets in Section 3 will actually be verified.\n119\t\n120\t## 15. Rollout, Migration, and Rollback\n121\t\n122\t- How the system reaches users: feature flags, staged or percentage rollout, beta groups.\n123\t- For changes to existing systems: how old and new run side by side, the steps for migrating data, and the switchover criteria.\n124\t- The rollback procedure for each risky step, and the point after which rolling back is no longer possible.\n125\t\n126\t## 16. Risks and Mitigations\n127\t\n128\tA table with the columns *risk*, *likelihood*, *impact*, *mitigation*, *early warning sign*, and *owner*. Include technical, delivery, dependency, and organisational risks.\n129\t\n130\t## 17. Deferred Work and Future Evolution\n131\t\n132\t- Items deliberately postponed, and what would trigger building each one.\n133\t- Ways the architecture is expected to evolve, and the extension points that support it.\n134\t- Known shortcuts or technical debt taken on purpose, with a plan to pay each one back.\n135\t\n136\t## 18. Next Steps\n137\t\n138\tThree to seven actions someone can take immediately. These include answering the open questions that block progress and starting the first tasks. Name the specific files, commands, or people where possible.\n139\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"eabe0796-3222-4be1-beca-8d837128483f","uuid":"6693a25e-18bc-4f79-a616-62d279707553","timestamp":"2026-10-02T23:47:59.947Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p2ab33809\\skills\\architecture-planner\\reference\\document-template.md","content":"# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n\nUse the sections below in this order. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01SA68ju88mLQ5Av9WgBUS2y","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections that are relevant. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n4\t\n5\t## 1. Discovery questions\n6\t\n7\tChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n8\t\n9\t- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n10\t- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n11\t- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n12\t- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n13\t- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n14\t- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n15\t- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n16\t- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n17\t- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n18\t- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n19\t\n20\t## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n21\t\n22\t| Attribute | Express it as |\n23\t|---|---|\n24\t| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n25\t| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n26\t| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n27\t| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n28\t| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n29\t| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n30\t| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n31\t| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n32\t| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n33\t\n34\tIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n35\t\n36\t## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n37\t\n38\t- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n39\t- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n40\t- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n41\t- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n42\t- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n43\t- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n44\t- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n45\t\n46\t## 4. Data checklist\n47\t\n48\t- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n49\t- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n50\t- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n51\t- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n52\t- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n53\t- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n54\t- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n55\t- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n56\t\n57\t## 5. Choosing technology\n58\t\n59\t- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n60\t- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n61\t- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n62\t- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n63\t- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n64\t- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n65\t\n66\t## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n67\t\n68\t- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n69\t- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n70\t- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n71\t- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n72\t- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n73\t- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n74\t- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n75\t\n76\t## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n77\t\n78\tA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n79\t\n80\t- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n81\t- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n82\t- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n83\t- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n84\t\n85\tKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n86\t\n87\t## 8. Security checklist\n88\t\n89\t- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n90\t- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n91\t- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n92\t- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n93\t- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n94\t- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n95\t- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n96\t- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n97\t- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n98\t\n99\t## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n100\t\n101\t- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n102\t- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n103\t- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n104\t- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n105\t- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n106\t- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n107\t- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n108\t- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n109\t- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n110\t\n111\t## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n112\t\n113\t- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n114\t- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n115\t- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n116\t- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n117\t- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n118\t- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n119\t- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n120\t- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n121\t- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n122\t- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n123\t- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Infrastructure checklist\n127\t\n128\t- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n129\t- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n130\t- Remote infrastructure state with locking. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n\n## 1. Discovery questions\n\nChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n\n- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n\n## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n\n| Attribute | Express it as |\n|---|---|\n| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n\nIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n\n## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n\n- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n\n## 4. Data checklist\n\n- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n\n## 5. Choosing technology\n\n- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n\n## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n\n- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n\n## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n\nA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n\n- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n\nKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n\n## 8. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. A plan for applying patches.\n- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n\n## 9. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n\n## 12. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n\n## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n\n- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n","numLines":157,"startLine":1,"totalLines":157}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_fegsz377osubcgtlr3l7lhwpuugu3r2xvjjzk6sby5xzy52ph7qq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# CI/CD Platform for 50 Microservices: Architecture and Build Sequence\n\n> **Before you read:** The workspace has no existing code or config (`README.md` says it is intentionally empty), so I couldn't check what you run today. The plan rests on stated defaults: GitHub, AWS, Kubernetes, 50 services in separate repos, existing ad-hoc pipelines, a platform team of 4–5, and SOC 2-style compliance. They are listed in §5. Five answers would change the plan the most; they're at the end, each with the default I used. The sequencing (§12–13) holds up well even if the defaults are wrong. The tool choices in §10 are what would change.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** A shared CI/CD platform: a standard path from commit to production that all 50 microservices can use. Platform engineers build it and product teams use it. It replaces today's mix of pipelines.\n- **Shape:** Each service repo has a short config file that calls **versioned shared pipeline templates** (`platform-pipelines`). These templates build, test, scan, sign, and push one image per commit. Deploys use **GitOps**: CI records the image digest (the image's unique content hash) in a `deploy-config` repo. Argo CD, running in each cluster, pulls changes from that repo and applies them. CI never holds credentials for the clusters.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. GitHub Actions reusable workflows, not a custom-built orchestrator.\n  2. A pull-based GitOps deploy with Argo CD, one instance per cluster, not CI pushing to clusters.\n  3. Build once and promote the same signed image digest through dev, staging, and prod.\n  4. Template versions are pinned in each repo and upgraded by automated PRs, so one bad template change can't break all 50 services.\n  5. GitHub-hosted runners to start, with self-hosted runners only if a spike shows we need them.\n- **The real critical path is migration throughput, not platform features.** Building the platform takes roughly 10 weeks. Moving 50 services onto it takes 5–7 months more and depends on product teams having time.\n- **Milestone 1 (about 4–6 weeks):** One real service goes from commit to production through the new path, with a timed rollback drill. It also includes a full inventory of the 50 services and four spikes (time-boxed experiments): rollback with database migrations, template versioning, runner choice, and secrets.\n- **Top risks:**\n  - A long tail of special-case pipelines with undocumented behaviour.\n  - Product teams not having time for migration.\n  - One template change breaking many services at once.\n  - The CI system becoming the easiest route to attack production.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem (assumed):** 50 services built and deployed by a mix of Jenkins jobs, per-repo scripts, and some manual steps. Each team maintains its own pipeline. Security controls (scanning, approvals, audit trail) are inconsistent. Rollback depends on who is on call. Lead time and failure rates aren't measured.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Every service ships through one supported path.\n  - Every production change can be traced to a reviewed commit and a signed image.\n  - Rollback is a single, well-practised action.\n  - Teams onboard themselves.\n- **Non-goals (for this plan):**\n  - Per-PR preview environments.\n  - An internal developer portal (e.g. Backstage).\n  - Multi-region deployment.\n  - Monorepo build-graph tooling.\n  - Replacing service teams' own test suites.\n  - Infrastructure provisioning for services (databases, queues).\n- **Success measures:**\n  - At least 48 of 50 services in production on the platform, and legacy CI shut down, within about 9 months.\n  - Standard service onboarding takes 2 engineer-days or less from the service team.\n  - DORA metrics (deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore) are measured for 100% of services from M3 onward.\n  - Median lead time from commit to production is under 1 day.\n  - Production rollback takes under 10 minutes.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes** (all targets are assumptions until confirmed):\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it ranks here |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Production change safety | 100% of prod changes come from a reviewed git commit with a signed image digest. Rollback takes under 10 minutes. CI has no long-lived cloud keys. | A shared platform also concentrates risk: one flaw affects 50 services. We'll accept slower pipelines (by minutes) to get this. |\n| 2 | Migration throughput / adoption | 50 services migrated in ≤ 9 months. A standard service onboards in ≤ 2 engineer-days. | The platform delivers nothing until services are on it. Running two systems side by side doubles operating cost. |\n| 3 | Small blast radius for platform changes | No more than 1 platform-caused breakage per month that hits more than 3 services. | Templates are shared code running in 50 places. |\n| 4 | Developer feedback speed | PR checks p95 under 10 minutes. Merge to dev p95 under 20 minutes. | Slow pipelines get bypassed, which undermines #1 and #2. |\n| 5 | Operability and cost | Run by the platform team without 24/7 on-call for the platform itself. Platform run cost of about $3–8k/month, excluding clusters. | Small team. Managed and hosted options are preferred. |\n\n**Key functional requirements:**\n- One pipeline template for each language stack.\n- Image build, test, vulnerability scan, SBOM (software bill of materials, a list of what's inside the image), and signing.\n- Promotion from dev to staging to prod with gates.\n- Hooks for database migrations.\n- Standard Kubernetes packaging (deployment settings).\n- Secret injection at runtime.\n- Canary rollout for tier-1 services.\n- Pipeline and DORA metrics.\n\n**Constraints (assumed):**\n- GitHub (Cloud or Enterprise), AWS, and existing EKS clusters for dev, staging, and prod.\n- 3–4 language stacks.\n- Platform team of 4–5 who know Kubernetes and Terraform but are new to Argo CD.\n- About 10–12 product teams own the services.\n\n**Hard parts:**\n\n| Hard part | Why it's hard |\n|---|---|\n| H1. The long tail of special-case services | Legacy jobs quietly do things like running migrations, warming caches, or tagging tickets. The last 10 services will take as long as the first 40. |\n| H2. Rollback with database migrations | Git-revert rollback is only safe if schema changes work with the previous release. That's a convention the platform can't enforce alone. |\n| H3. Template versioning across 50 repos | Fixed version pins mean upgrades need constant PRs. Floating versions mean one bad change breaks everything. |\n| H4. CI as a route to production | A compromised third-party action or a fork PR on a privileged runner could reach the registry or prod. |\n| H5. Product-team capacity | Migration work competes with feature work. Without agreed time from product teams, migration waves stall. |\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nNothing was available to inspect; the workspace is empty. Assumed:\n- About 50 service repos on GitHub.\n- A mix of Jenkins and GitHub Actions pipelines.\n- Helm or raw manifests applied by CI using cluster credentials.\n- Secrets in a mix of Jenkins credentials, CI variables, and AWS Secrets Manager.\n- Some services run their database migrations inside deploy scripts.\n\n**The M1 inventory (T2) replaces these assumptions with facts.** Treat any section that relies on them as provisional until T2 is done.\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n| Assumption | Impact if wrong | How and when it's checked |\n|---|---|---|\n| A1. Code is on GitHub | GitLab swaps in CI/CD Components and GitLab runners. The structure stays; the tooling changes. | Answer to Q1, before T3 |\n| A2. All services run on Kubernetes (EKS) | VMs/ECS/Lambda break the GitOps/Argo CD design and would need a push-deploy path for those services. | T2 inventory, week 1 |\n| A3. One repo per service | A monorepo needs change-detection logic (Nx/Bazel/path filters), and the \"template per repo\" model changes. | Q3, before T7 |\n| A4. Compliance accepts an approved PR as the change record (no manual change board) | If a change board is required, prod promotion needs a step that creates a change ticket, plus checks that the author and approver are different people. | Q4 / T1 security review, week 2 |\n| A5. Platform team of 4–5, plus 1–3 days per service from product teams | All timelines scale with this. | Q5, week 1 |\n| A6. GitHub-hosted runners can reach everything builds need | Self-hosted runners (Actions Runner Controller, ARC) move into M2, adding about 2–3 weeks. | Spike S3, week 2–3 |\n| A7. There are separate dev, staging, and prod clusters | Argo CD topology and promotion layout change. | T2, week 1 |\n| A8. About 10 services are tier-1 (critical, customer-facing) | Changes the size of Wave 2 and how much canary work is needed. | T2, week 1 |\n\nOpen questions with owners, defaults, and deadlines are in the **closing section**.\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  devr[Developer] -->|push / PR| svc\n  subgraph GH[\"GitHub (CI trust zone - no cluster credentials)\"]\n    svc[\"Service repo x50<br/>.github/workflows/ci.yml\"]\n    pp[\"platform-pipelines<br/>reusable workflows @vX.Y\"]\n    run[\"GitHub-hosted runners\"]\n    dc[\"deploy-config repo<br/>apps/&lt;svc&gt;/&lt;env&gt;/values.yaml\"]\n    pc[\"platform-charts<br/>shared 'service' Helm chart\"]\n    svc -->|uses| pp\n    svc --> run\n  end\n  run -->|OIDC to push-only IAM role| ecr[(\"ECR<br/>images, SBOMs, signatures\")]\n  run -->|GitHub App: commit / PR| dc\n  subgraph DEV[dev cluster]\n    ad[Argo CD]\n  end\n  subgraph STG[staging cluster]\n    as[Argo CD]\n  end\n  subgraph PRD[\"prod cluster (separate trust zone)\"]\n    ap[Argo CD] --> wl[Workloads]\n    ky[Kyverno policies]\n    eso[External Secrets] --> sm[(Secrets Manager)]\n  end\n  ad & as & ap -->|pull| dc\n  ad & as & ap -->|pull| pc\n  wl -->|pull by digest| ecr\n  ap -.metrics.-> obs[(Existing metrics stack)]\n  run -.run events.-> obs\n```\n\n**How it fits together:**\n1. A service repo has a roughly 20-line `ci.yml` that calls `platform-pipelines` workflows pinned to a version.\n2. The build produces one signed image digest.\n3. The promote workflow writes that digest into `deploy-config` for the target environment.\n4. Each cluster's Argo CD notices the change and syncs the shared `service` chart with the service's values.\n5. Kyverno checks signatures when pods are admitted.\n6. External Secrets brings in runtime secrets. Secrets never pass through CI.\n\n**Trust boundaries:**\n- CI can push images and write to `deploy-config`, but it can't reach clusters.\n- The prod paths in `deploy-config` are protected by CODEOWNERS and required checks.\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Interfaces | Technology | Key dependencies |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `platform-pipelines` | Shared build/test/scan/sign/push and promote logic | Template code, release tags | `workflow_call` inputs and outputs (semver) | GitHub Actions reusable workflows and composite actions | GitHub, ECR |\n| Service `ci.yml` (×50) | Per-service config: stack, test command, which environments | None beyond config | Calls templates | YAML | `platform-pipelines` |\n| `platform-charts/service` | Standard K8s packaging: probes, resources, HPA, PDB, labels, optional migration Job | Chart versions | Helm values schema (semver) | Helm 3 + `values.schema.json` | — |\n| `deploy-config` | **System of record for desired state** in each environment | Digest and values per service and environment | Git commits/PRs, validation checks | Git + Argo CD ApplicationSet | GitHub |\n| Argo CD (one per cluster) | Applies desired state, detects drift, reports health | Sync status (can be rebuilt from git) | Git pull, UI/API, Prometheus metrics | Argo CD (HA in prod) | `deploy-config`, ECR |\n| ECR | Stores artifacts | Images, SBOMs, signatures | OCI registry | AWS ECR, immutable tags | AWS IAM |\n| Kyverno | Admission policy: signed images only, required labels/limits | Policies (in git) | K8s admission webhook | Kyverno | ECR (signature lookup) |\n| External Secrets Operator | Runtime secret sync | None (Secrets Manager is the source) | `ExternalSecret` CRD | ESO + AWS Secrets Manager | IAM roles for service accounts |\n| `platform-infra` | IAM/OIDC, ECR repos, Argo CD install, runner config | Terraform state (S3 + DynamoDB lock) | Terraform PRs | Terraform | AWS, GitHub provider |\n| Pipeline metrics exporter | Pipeline duration and outcome, DORA | Time-series data | GitHub webhooks/API to metrics store | Small scheduled job, or off-the-shelf exporter | Existing Prometheus/Grafana (assumed) |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**`platform-pipelines`** (the hard parts here are H3 and H4)\n- **Releases:** semver tags (`v1.4.2`) plus a moving major tag (`v1`). Service repos pin a full version. Renovate opens upgrade PRs, so the service's own CI tests each template upgrade before it's merged. That limits a bad change to repos that merge it.\n- **Contents:** `build.yml`, `promote.yml`, and composite actions `setup-<lang>`, `scan`, `sign`.\n- **Not its job:** running service-specific integration suites. It calls the service's `make test` / `make integration`.\n- **Escape hatch:** a `pre-build`/`post-test` hook input. If a service needs more than that, it's a signal to add a template feature, not to fork.\n- **Load:** about 50 repos × 10–20 runs a day.\n- **Failure handling:** a template bug shows up as a failed Renovate PR in a canary repo, and the release is yanked (tag deleted, patch released).\n\n**`deploy-config`**\n- **Layout:** `apps/<svc>/{dev,staging,prod}/values.yaml` (containing `image.digest` and environment overrides), plus `apps/<svc>/base.yaml`.\n- **Argo applications:** an ApplicationSet in each cluster creates one Argo Application per `apps/*/<env>`.\n- **Write rules:**\n  - Dev: the promote workflow commits directly.\n  - Staging: PR with auto-merge once checks pass.\n  - Prod: PR needing approval from the service's CODEOWNERS.\n- **Required checks:**\n  - `helm template` + kubeconform.\n  - Kyverno CLI policy test.\n  - `cosign verify` that the digest was signed by the `platform-pipelines` workflow identity.\n  - **Promotion-order check:** a prod digest must currently be healthy in staging.\n- **Failure:** if GitHub is down, nothing new deploys, but running workloads aren't affected (Argo keeps the last applied state). The break-glass procedure is in §9 Flow 4.\n\n**Argo CD:** one instance per cluster, so prod credentials never leave prod.\n- Auto-sync with self-heal in every environment, so git is the only way to make changes.\n- Manual UI sync is restricted to the on-call role.\n- Prod runs in HA mode (redis-ha, 2+ repo-servers).\n- The instance holds no state that can't be rebuilt from git, so recovery is \"reinstall from `platform-infra` and resync\".\n\n**`platform-charts/service`:** one chart covering about 90% of services.\n- Optional `migration` Job, run as an Argo PreSync hook (it runs before the new version rolls out).\n- From M4: an optional `Rollout` object (Argo Rollouts) for canaries.\n- Values schema is checked by `values.schema.json`. A major version bump is needed for any breaking change to values.\n- Services that don't fit can supply raw manifests (`apps/<svc>/manifests/`), tracked as a known exception.\n\n**ECR / Kyverno / ESO:** routine.\n- ECR: immutable tags, scan on push, lifecycle rules (§8).\n- Kyverno: `verifyImages` runs in **audit** mode until M5 and switches to **enforce** once all services are signed.\n\n**Runners:** GitHub-hosted, with larger runners for heavy builds. Docker layer cache goes to ECR with `cache-to type=registry`. Fork PRs get read-only tokens and no OIDC role.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n| Entity | System of record | Writer | Retention | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Pipeline definitions | `platform-pipelines`, service repos | Platform / service teams via PR | Forever (git) | — |\n| Desired deploy state | `deploy-config` | `promote.yml` (GitHub App), humans via PR | Forever (git). Git history is the audit trail. | Exactly one writer path per environment (above) |\n| Images, SBOMs, signatures | ECR | `build.yml` only (push-only role) | Untagged: 14 days. Non-prod digests: 90 days. **Any digest ever deployed to prod: ≥ 1 year** (assumed; confirm with compliance) | Immutable. Referenced by digest, never by `latest`. |\n| Live sync and health | Argo CD (derived) | Argo CD | Rebuilt from git | Not backed up on purpose |\n| Pipeline run history | GitHub | GitHub | 90 days in GitHub. Summaries exported to the metrics store for 13 months. | Source for DORA |\n| Runtime secrets | AWS Secrets Manager | Service teams / Terraform | Per secret policy | Never in git, images, or CI logs |\n| Terraform state | S3 + DynamoDB lock | `platform-infra` pipeline | Versioned bucket | Split by env and component to limit blast radius |\n\n- **Consistency:** the only invariant that matters is that prod only runs digests that went through staging. The `deploy-config` required check enforces it at write time, not by a later reconciliation.\n- **Backups:**\n  - Git repos are mirrored nightly to an S3 bucket in the platform's AWS account (protects against GitHub account loss).\n  - ECR is durable. Cross-region replication is deferred (§17).\n- **Schema evolution:** the chart values schema follows semver. Breaking chart changes ship as a new major version, and services move over through Renovate PRs to `deploy-config`.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**Flow 1: Commit to production (happy path)**\n1. A PR on `orders-svc` runs `build.yml@v1.4.2`: lint, unit tests, build, and Trivy scan (fails on critical vulnerabilities that have a fix). No push for PRs from forks.\n2. On merge to `main`, `build.yml` builds, generates an SBOM with syft, signs keyless with cosign (via GitHub OIDC), and pushes `ecr/orders-svc@sha256:abc…`.\n3. `promote.yml env=dev` commits the digest to `apps/orders-svc/dev/values.yaml`. Argo CD in dev syncs. The workflow waits until Argo reports `Healthy` and runs the service's smoke target. Elapsed time: 20 minutes or less.\n4. `promote.yml env=staging` opens a PR. Checks pass, it auto-merges, Argo syncs, and the smoke tests pass.\n5. `promote.yml env=prod` opens a PR. The checks verify the signature and that the digest is healthy in staging. A service CODEOWNER approves, and the PR merges.\n6. If the chart has a `migration` Job, it runs as a PreSync hook. Then the rollout proceeds. Kyverno checks the signature when pods are admitted.\n\n**Flow 2: Bad release in production (rollback)**\n1. Error rates climb after the prod sync. On-call runs `promote.yml env=prod digest=<previous>`, or reverts the prod commit in `deploy-config`. Either is a single PR with an expedited approval rule for on-call.\n2. Argo syncs the previous digest. Target: under 10 minutes from decision to healthy.\n3. **This is safe only if** the migration was additive (expand/contract: add the new schema first, remove the old one in a later release), so the previous release still works with the new schema. Spike S1 tests whether that holds. If it doesn't, the plan adds a per-service \"migration compatibility\" gate (§13, S1).\n\n**Flow 3: A bad template release (blast-radius failure path)**\n1. The platform team tags `v1.5.0` with a bug in the cache step. Fixture repos pass, because the bug only shows up with a Gradle feature that the fixtures don't use.\n2. Renovate opens upgrade PRs. Canary repos (5 volunteer services) get them first. Other repos get them only after 48 hours, using Renovate's `minimumReleaseAge` setting.\n3. A canary repo's upgrade PR fails CI and can't merge. The platform alert (\"template upgrade PR failure rate > 20%\") fires.\n4. The `v1.5.0` tag is withdrawn, `v1.5.1` is released, and a fixture covering the Gradle case is added. Result: no production impact, one canary team's PR is blocked for a few hours, and the other 45 services never see `v1.5.0`.\n\n**Flow 4: GitHub outage during an incident**\n1. Argo CD can't fetch, but current workloads keep running.\n2. If an urgent prod fix is needed, on-call uses the break-glass role: an audited IAM role with time-limited access to Argo CD in prod.\n3. They set the Application's target revision, or patch the image to a **digest already in ECR**, and record the action. Argo self-heal is paused for that app only.\n4. Afterwards, git is updated to match, and self-heal is turned back on.\n5. The procedure is rehearsed once in M3.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| Decision | Options considered | Rationale (against drivers) | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| D1. CI engine: GitHub Actions reusable workflows | (a) GHA; (b) keep Jenkins with shared libraries; (c) Tekton or a custom orchestrator | Code is already on GitHub (A1). Native OIDC (#1), no CI servers to run (#5), the PR experience teams already know (#2). Jenkins means running controllers and plugins. Tekton means building a product. | Medium. Templates can be ported; service `ci.yml` files are small. | The org is on GitLab, or GHA limits (e.g. reusable workflow nesting depth) block the template design in S2 |\n| D2. Deploy model: GitOps pull with Argo CD, one per cluster | (a) Argo CD per cluster; (b) a central Argo CD managing all clusters; (c) CI runs `helm upgrade` (push) | No cluster credentials in CI (#1). Rollback is a git revert (#1). Drift detection. Per-cluster keeps prod credentials inside prod. The cost of new tooling is accepted and budgeted at 1–2 weeks of learning in M1. | **Hard.** It sets the trust model and what every team does day to day. | Services aren't on Kubernetes (A2), or there are more than about 10 clusters (move to a hub-and-spoke model) |\n| D3. Build once, promote the digest | (a) One digest everywhere; (b) rebuild per environment | Guarantees prod runs what was tested. Signing becomes meaningful. | Hard to undo culturally, easy technically | Never, realistically |\n| D4. Template distribution: pinned semver plus Renovate with staged release | (a) Pinned + Renovate; (b) floating `@v1`; (c) copy-paste starter pipelines | (a) limits blast radius (#3) while keeping upgrades cheap. (b) breaks 50 services at once. (c) drifts within months. | Easy | S2 shows Renovate noise is unacceptable. Fallback: floating `@v1` for most repos plus a `@canary` channel. |\n| D5. Packaging: shared `service` Helm chart plus a raw-manifest exception path | (a) Shared chart; (b) a Kustomize base per service; (c) every team writes its own chart | Standard probes, limits, and labels for everyone (#1, #2). Less to review. | Medium | More than 20% of services need the exception path |\n| D6. Runners: GitHub-hosted first | (a) Hosted (larger runners where needed); (b) self-hosted ephemeral ARC on a build cluster | Nothing to operate (#5). The pull-based deploy means CI doesn't need private network access. Roughly $2–6k/month (see §11). | Easy | S3 shows p95 build over 15 minutes with caching, a need for private network access, or cost over about $8k/month |\n| D7. Prod approval: CODEOWNER approval on the `deploy-config` PR | (a) Git PR approval as the change record; (b) an extra change-board ticket step | Auditable, fast (#4), lives where engineers already work | Easy | Compliance requires a change board or stricter separation of duties (Q4). Then add a ticket-creating check to the prod PR. |\n| D8. Secrets: External Secrets Operator from AWS Secrets Manager | (a) ESO; (b) secrets injected by CI; (c) Sealed Secrets in git | Secrets stay out of CI entirely (#1) and can be rotated | Medium | The org already mandates Vault (ESO supports Vault, so it's a small change) |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n**Security** (H4)\n- **Built in M1:**\n  - GitHub OIDC to AWS with a push-only role, restricted by repo and by `ref:refs/heads/main`.\n  - No static keys anywhere.\n  - A GitHub App with write access to `deploy-config` only.\n  - Third-party actions pinned by SHA, enforced by a lint check in `platform-pipelines` CI.\n  - Fork PRs get read-only tokens and no OIDC.\n  - Keyless signing with cosign.\n  - Secret scanning and push protection turned on.\n- **M3:**\n  - Kyverno `verifyImages` in audit mode.\n  - Branch protection and CODEOWNERS on every `deploy-config/apps/*/prod`.\n  - GitHub audit log streamed to the security log store.\n- **M5:** Kyverno switched to enforce mode, and `kubectl` write access to prod removed from humans except the break-glass role.\n\n| Threat | Mitigation |\n|---|---|\n| A compromised third-party action steals tokens | SHA pinning, a list of approved actions, short-lived OIDC tokens with narrow scope |\n| A malicious PR runs on privileged CI | Fork PRs get no secrets or OIDC. `pull_request_target` is banned in templates. |\n| An unreviewed image reaches prod | Only the promote path writes to `deploy-config`. Prod requires CODEOWNER approval and a signature check at both PR time and admission. |\n| Leaked long-lived cloud keys | None exist. Credential reports are checked in M1 exit criteria. |\n| A vulnerable dependency ships | Trivy gate on critical vulnerabilities that have a fix. SBOM stored so later CVE lookups are possible. |\n\n**Reliability**\n- Platform target: 99.5% of business hours for the \"merge to dev\" path, measured by the synthetic `platform-canary` service (§14).\n- Running workloads never depend on CI being up.\n- Promote steps are idempotent: writing the same digest twice is a no-op commit, which is skipped.\n- `promote.yml` waits for Argo health with a 15-minute timeout, then fails and alerts. It never retries a deploy blindly.\n- Argo CD runs in HA mode in prod (M3).\n\n**Observability**\n- **Built in M1:** pipeline run duration and outcome per workflow and stage, exported to the existing metrics stack (T11). Argo CD Prometheus metrics.\n- **M3:**\n  - DORA dashboard per service and team.\n  - Alerts on symptoms, each linked to a runbook in `platform-pipelines/docs/runbooks/`:\n    - `platform-canary` hasn't reached dev in 60 minutes.\n    - Template-upgrade PR failure rate over 20%.\n    - An Argo app in prod `Degraded` or `OutOfSync` for more than 15 minutes.\n    - Pipeline queue time p95 over 5 minutes.\n\n**Performance and capacity**\n- **Expected load:** about 750–1,000 workflow runs a day at peak, with bursts when a Renovate wave lands.\n- **Likely bottlenecks:** GitHub concurrent-job limits, ECR API rate limits, and cache misses.\n- **Load test (before M3 wave 1):** trigger 50 builds at the same time and check queue time and ECR throttling.\n\n**Cost** (rough, assumed)\n- Runner minutes: about 150–250k a month. At GitHub's current list prices that's roughly $1.5–6k/month, depending on how many jobs use larger runners. **Check against current GitHub pricing before you budget.**\n- ECR storage: low hundreds of dollars.\n- Argo CD and Kyverno run on existing clusters, so small marginal cost.\n- **Controls:**\n  - `concurrency` with cancel-in-progress on PRs.\n  - Path filters.\n  - Registry layer cache.\n  - Monthly cost review per repo using GitHub usage reports.\n  - Budget alert at $8k (the D6 revisit trigger).\n\n**Operations**\n- **The platform team owns:** templates, the chart, Argo CD, Kyverno, `deploy-config` structure, and runner config.\n- **Service teams own:** their `ci.yml`, tests, values, migrations, and deploy health.\n- **On-call:**\n  - Platform on-call during business hours from M3. Out of hours, Argo CD/GitHub issues use the break-glass runbook, with best-effort escalation.\n  - Service incidents stay with service on-call.\n- **Support:** a `#platform-help` channel plus office hours during migration waves.\n\n**AI-specific concerns:** not applicable. There are no model-driven components.\n\n## 12. Build Sequence\n\n**Team assumption for sizing:** 4–5 platform engineers. Product teams spend 1–3 engineer-days per standard service and 1–2 weeks per special-case service. Ranges are rough guides, not commitments.\n\n```\nWeeks:     1    5    10   15   20   25   30   35\nM1 Slice   ████\nM2 Golden       █████\nM3 Wave1            ██████   (+ hardening track in parallel)\nM4 Wave2                  ███████ (+ canary for tier-1)\nM5 Tail                          ████████ (+ enforce, decommission)\nCritical path: access/IAM → M1 slice → template v1 stable (M2) → wave capacity (M3–M5) → legacy CI off\n```\n\n| Milestone | Goal / risk cleared | Scope (in / **out**) | Deliverables | Exit criteria | Dependencies | Rough size |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **M1: Thin slice to prod** | Proves the whole path (GitOps, OIDC, signing, promotion, rollback) on one real service. Answers H2, H3, H4 and the runner question. Replaces assumptions with the inventory. | In: one pilot service, all three environments, spikes S1–S4. **Out:** canary, Kyverno enforcement, other stacks, DORA dashboards. | `platform-pipelines` v0.x, `service` chart v0.x, `deploy-config`, Argo CD ×3, OIDC/ECR Terraform, inventory, 4 spike write-ups | Pilot deployed to prod through the platform at least 5 times. Rollback timed under 10 minutes in staging and once in prod. No static AWS keys in any pilot CI. Inventory 50/50 confirmed by owners. Spike decisions recorded as ADRs (architecture decision records). | Long-lead access (T1) on day 1 | 4–6 weeks |\n| **M2: Golden path v1 + pilots** | Proves the templates work beyond one service: each stack, one service with a DB, and the worst-looking special case from the inventory. Makes onboarding self-service. | In: 4 more pilot services (one per remaining stack, plus one special case), template `v1.0.0`, Renovate staged release, fixture test harness, onboarding guide and `ci.yml` scaffold. ARC only if S3 calls for it. **Out:** tier-1 services. | `v1.0.0` templates, `service` chart `v1.0.0`, `docs/onboarding.md`, fixture repos, parity checklist | 5 services in prod on the platform. A product team onboards a service from the guide in 2 days or less without platform help (observed once). A template release reaches canary repos, then the rest, via Renovate. | M1 | 5–7 weeks (+2–3 if ARC is needed) |\n| **M3: Wave 1 (≈12 tier-3/tier-2 services) + hardening track** | Tests migration throughput with low-risk services. Makes the platform safe enough for tier-1. | Wave: 12 services, mostly migrated by their own teams with platform pairing. Hardening: Argo CD HA, Kyverno audit mode, DORA dashboard, alerts and runbooks, break-glass drill, 50-concurrent-build load test, platform business-hours on-call. **Out:** tier-1 services. | 17 services on the platform, dashboards, runbooks, drill report | 17/50 services.
